en: Discerning Errors (Discerning the errors in the Illustrations of the Six Requisites).
Narrated by the Śramaṇa Miaosheng of Kuaiji.
The regulations for the three robes and six requisites are concise and stem from the Buddha’s own mind; their merit is indeed immeasurable. Thereupon, [the author] explains:

You must not, for even a moment, neglect or forget these regulations; yet, throughout the Qi dynasty, there have been those who did not follow the teachings, and I, Y愚, have long desired to rectify this but have not yet been able to do so.
One day, Vinaya Master Dongzang produced a separate "Diagram of the Six Objects" (liuwu tu) with the intent of reforming these abuses.
When I first heard of it, I was greatly pleased and consequently sought out the original to examine it. Unfortunately, its...
In this interim work, there are many omissions and errors in both text and meaning; consequently, my own mind remains somewhat uneasy.

Thus, I have extensively set forth points within the diagrams and texts that were not yet fully realized, while also correcting errors based on my own observations and learning. My primary aim has been to preserve these insights herein.
It is not that I delight in altering the words of others or asserting them to be different; rather, I merely fear that their explanations might circulate separately in the world.
Those who rely solely on faith have consequently failed to consult the commentaries and the main text;

thus, as days and months have gradually passed, errors have been transmitted for so long that they can no longer be rectified. Yet, was it appropriate to remain silent at the very inception of this matter?

I pray that you will examine my humble and limited views against the diagrams and texts: what do they truly say? If, however, you remain resolutely unwilling to follow them, how [can this be justified]?

In this world today, there are no such people; thus, I have briefly composed these eleven sections. As for the lack of sequential order in the text, it is because I followed the sequence of the diagrams and passages, identifying and explaining them as they appeared.
There are several other points remaining, which I have omitted here to avoid prolixity.
Establishing titles leads to verbal excess; drawing diagrams is useless. Worldly talk obscures the Way; discarding robes is merely a sectarian label.

To accept [offerings] is not called "threefold relinquishment," nor is it called "single relinquishment. Clarifying appearances exposes frivolous proliferation; altering the text to suit oneself ruins the ritual mat.
Abolishing the *zēng* (additional) and using a pouch to distinguish the ties—I urge the abandonment of such diagrams and texts.
Regarding the title "A Diagram of the Six Requisites for Bhikṣus as Instituted by the Buddha" (首題曰佛制比丘六物圖), the critique states:
"I have long heard of the 'six requisites for bhikṣus instituted by the Buddha,' yet I have never heard of a 'diagram' being among those instituted by the Buddha.
The word 'diagram' (圖) is merely human terminology; how can it be said that this is 'a diagram of the six requisites for bhikṣus instituted by the Buddha'?"

"Is this not a case where the title is established with such ambiguity that gold and stone cannot be distinguished? Or perhaps someone says: 'The single character "tu" (diagram) is the name established for the present work;
it certainly cannot be read as being governed by the two characters "fo-zhi" (Buddha-ordinance). I say: Not so.
That person merely wishes to force a distinction, yet the phrasing itself resists such division. How can one rely upon such arbitrary assertions? How could this be?

In works such as the *Nanshan Jietan Tujing* (Diagram Sutra of the Nanshan Ordination Platform), the *Zhufa Tuzan* (Illustrated Praise of the Abiding Dharma), and the *Guidu Tujing* (Diagram Sutra of Ritual Standards), the phrase "established by the Buddha" (*fuzhi*) does not appear.
Some say that because the six requisites (*liuwu*) were established solely by the Buddha, the term "established by the Buddha" was used for them alone. To this I reply:

But the ordination platform (*jietan*) was also established by the Buddha; why then did the Master of the Nanshan [Daoxuan] not refer to it as the "Buddha-established Ordination Platform Sutra"? From this we know that...
It is truly difficult to establish a single topic for a single work; you have now taken up the brush and encountered this difficulty before even ten or twenty characters have passed.
How much more so, then, for the treatises and commentaries composed by the former masters that circulate widely in the world—how many errors could they not contain?
"Drawing diagrams is of no benefit" (referring to the six types of diagrams where the upper part labels the *saṃghāṭī* and so forth, while the lower part depicts their forms).
Bian said: "In these diagrams, one can see the number of strips, such as the twenty-five-fold [robe], but I have not heard of the merit of the actual methods for manufacturing them.
Furthermore, the cloth for robes may be single or double-layered; the hooks and ties may be at the front or back; and the seams may be 'bird-foot' or 'horse-[hoof]' shaped."

Regarding the distinctions of the teeth, the diagram does not clearly manifest their characteristics; it merely transcribes the text of the *Gantong zhuan* (Account of Resonance and Response) in a straightforward manner.
If even those within the Vinaya school remain largely confused by this, how could others possibly understand it at once?
Furthermore, the essential point of donning robes lies in the hooks and ties (*gōuniù*); although the diagrams for the front and back show the edges receding downward...
In this rough explanation, it was not yet examined how far the boundaries of the left and right sides extend or how much they are removed;

since the text is not explicit, the diagram merely marks a few lines. If one simply draws the diagram, who cannot draw it? If one simply draws straight lines according to the text, who cannot draw them?
Have you not seen the *Nanshan Guidu Tu* (The Diagram of the Measurement Standards of Nanshan), which sketches the shape of a bell and counts the number of its successive hammers?
Furthermore, having transcribed verses and other texts beneath the illustrations, is this not equally beneficial?

Now, as for the fact that the text is superior [to the image], it is truly because one is timid regarding the composition and confused about the meaning; thus, what cannot be rendered level within the illustration is indeed impossible to do.
Since the illustrations are now of no benefit, and moreover, carving them into woodblocks for printing is merely laborious and...
[This is] useless.
It is a vulgar discourse that obscures the Way (the *Liùwù tújiàn* states: "The worldly tradition that the seven-strip vest and skirt constitute the three robes is erroneous").
My critique is: it may serve to correct the ignorant talk of the barbarians and the deaf, but it has no application here in the refined culture of this Middle Kingdom.
Regarding the nature of things, how could those who have left the household life not know the names of the three robes? For what reason is this known?

Furthermore, when one who has left the household life receives full ordination (*upasampadā*), the preceptor (*śikṣādātṛ*) and the instructor (*ācārya*) must certainly indicate the names of the robes;
would they ever mistakenly lead the candidate for ordination by referring to the seven-strip robe, the short-sleeved shirt, and the skirt as the "three robes"? It is only to be feared that...

Those who merely assume the outward form without receiving the precepts yet maintain such views—my son, you wield the pen to establish your words for posterity, opening paths of righteousness for others to supplement the Way.
Do not point out blind paths to the multitude; why present these shallow and vulgar expressions from worldly tradition onto paper and ink, only to invite derision from others?
Regarding the names of the three robes (trīṇi cīvarāṇi) as handed down by the world, you have correctly... [corrected them].
This is erroneous and makes it difficult to discern the correct path. Had not the Vinaya Master Dongzang corrected this, the names of the three robes throughout the world would remain unknown.

Regarding the classification of robe names (in the *Shiming*, under the section on robe names, the "Diagram and Textual Notes on Robes Worn When Entering Royal Palaces or Villages" states: "Worn when begging for food or preaching the Dharma").

Bian said: "The translation of the names is fundamentally universal, yet why is the interpretation of their meaning so restricted? Furthermore, when putting on robes to enter a village, one may do so whenever there are conditions such as those prescribed by the Dharma;
why single out the time for begging for food? If it is said that 'entering a village' refers to this [specific occasion], then it would imply entering at an improper time (*akāla*);

how could it be said that one enters specifically for the purpose of begging? If one were to rely solely on the time of begging for food, then conversely, it would clearly indicate that [other times] are improper."
When entering a village, it is not necessarily required to wear the *saṃghāṭī*. Furthermore, regarding the *uttarāsaṅga* being called the "garment for entering the assembly," a marginal note states:

"It is worn during rituals, chanting, and formal lectures. [The author] comments: This interpretation is also limited in scope. Moreover, when the community gathers, why would it be restricted only to the times of rituals, chanting, and formal lectures?

Instances such as the *pravāraṇā* ceremony and other occasions are followed by both the monastic community and private individuals alike; furthermore, this applies whenever there is the cultivation of goodness or the cessation of evil.

Regarding the phrase "when performing affairs or when things arise, one always wears the *xiàng* (formal robe) and enters the assembly," if this statement were based solely on the occasions of the *zhāi* (fasting) or lectures, then what clothing would one wear when entering the assembly during times such as the *zì* (recreational/ordinary) period?
Why is it not subsumed under the term "etcetera" (*děng*)? Therefore, the *Chāo* (Excerpts) quotes from the end of the *Wǔbǎiwèn jīng* (Sūtra of Five Hundred Questions), which says:
"Small robes that do not touch the body, provided they are clean and pure, may be worn when entering the assembly for meals, prostrations, and so forth. From this, we know [the meaning].

The word "etc. (*ādi*) includes everything without exception. Although this is a minor flaw, I fear that later students, taking this text as authoritative, will claim that one wearing the outer robe (*saṃghāṭī*) may enter a village at any time, not just during the proper hours, and that one wearing the inner robe (*antarvāsaka*) may enter any assembly at any time.
This would lead to great confusion among future generations, and the error would be significant.
Regarding the phrase "the acceptance does not mention 'three'": (in the section on the *cīvara-vidhi*, the three recitations are not indicated below).

Bian says: "The method of acceptance requires three recitations; if this is lacking, it is not established. This is because the text of the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* is limited, and thus it cannot be increased or decreased.
Now, since it does not mention 'three recitations,' I fear that perhaps even one recitation might suffice. [This is] for the sake of those who are confused."
Is it forgetfulness, or is it a deliberate exclusion? If you say it is a deliberate exclusion, it certainly does not require further discussion;

if you say it is due to forgetfulness, why must you open your mouth so wide to point out such an accusation as being excessive? To fail to consider another's perspective is truly something to be ashamed of.

Since his current composition is but one or two sheets of paper and yet contains the fault of confusion and obscurity, how much more so would this apply to the ten commentaries of the ancient masters?

That he has mastered the sutras is truly admirable; yet, though he wishes to compete with the commentaries and sub-commentaries in the world, he is unaware of the great error of misleading others and the failure to fulfill the requirements of the ritual—this is truly lamentable.
Even if one were to cut and tailor the robes according to the regulations, what would it matter if there were no formal method?
Regarding the statement that "in the act of relinquishing (*prahāṇa*), one does not say 'one'": [the *Śāyī-fǎ* (Method for Relinquishing Robes) below does not indicate saying it once].
Bian says: Since the method of receiving [the robes] requires three recitations while relinquishing requires only one, it is likely because receiving is difficult while relinquishing is easy.
Now, since the text does not state "one recitation," I fear that even three recitations might still be valid. Furthermore, the illustrations of the six requisites are scattered in all directions.

Those who lack clear understanding see that the *Śīlaskandha-vinaya* states there is no verbal formula for the relinquishment of robes, and they often claim that the act of relinquishing consists of either one recitation or three recitations, as if there were no fixed rule.
Relying solely on the words of the Vinaya Master Dongzang, they do not inquire further into why it does not say "one recitation," nor do they ask about the rest.
They know only to hastily utter the name [of the ritual] at the moment, failing to realize that the method for relinquishing and receiving the three robes has been once again mistaken.
It is also lamentable that this confusion has arisen among those who lack clarity.

Regarding "the appearance of light" (*prabhāta-lakṣaṇa*), it is a frivolous fabrication. (The diagram states that according to worldly tradition it is called "the light of Confucius," and others say it refers to "the appearance of light";
furthermore, the author himself adds a note stating that in the Vinaya, "light" refers to the break of dawn, while other claims regarding "leaking dust" and so forth are all erroneous.)
Bian said: "The explanations of Mingkong and others, though these are human words, do not fail to capture the meaning of 'tailoring and seeing the leaves.
I truly fear that the ancients made such statements because they wished people to understand easily.

Furthermore, while the expressions 'tailoring and seeing the leaves' and 'Ming Kong is equal to the sky' differ in being spoken by the ordinary and the sages respectively, they are nonetheless identical in their failure to grasp the meaning of the seamless seam."
Since the One does not obstruct the Great Principle, and furthermore is not manifested in paper or ink, why must one stubbornly cling to its terminology and dismiss it as erroneous?
Someone might say: "Is it not necessary to rectify names? How can one take a term used for a common meaning and indiscriminately conflate it with the words of a Sage?
I reply: This is not a matter of correcting the name of a garment; rather, it is the Sage clarifying its cutting and tailoring.
Because it refers to the appearance of sewing, it is called "tailoring" (*cai-feng*).

Although this is a conventional expression used by the world to refer to seeing leaves and such, it is intended to clarify the appearance of tailoring; thus, it is said that it clarifies the characteristics (*xiang-deng*).
If someone were to transmit the names "saṃghāṭī" and so forth while claiming that "clarifying the characteristics" is an error, that person would indeed be mistaken.

It must certainly be verified; how then could there be any question of correcting the terminology? Furthermore, you rebuke [the term] by saying that what is called the "appearance of light" (*prabhāta-nimitta*) at dawn is merely a matter of seeing leaves through a seam in one's clothing.
This again reveals the extreme narrowness and stubbornness of your perspective.

If you were to claim that because the common tradition of tailoring involves seeing leaves and calling it the "appearance of light," this is identical to the description of the "appearance of light at dawn" in the Vinaya, and thus you dismiss it as an error—[you would be mistaken].

The *Nanshan Guidu Tujing* (The Illustrated Scripture on the Measurement of the Southern Mountains) states that "the chanting of boundaries (*xiang*) originates from the leading [of the cord]," and it also says, "When discussing and chanting the boundaries, the proceedings then cease.
These points may likewise be used to refute [the current practice] by treating the terminology for chanting boundaries in the Vinaya as identical [to the ritual].
If this were the case, one would not only be refuting the worldly traditions using the Vinaya, but would also be attacking the sacred texts themselves as being both erroneous and corrupt.

Furthermore, one might think that the perilous nature of one's views and knowledge is being exposed to others; yet they do not realize that what is actually being exposed is the narrowness of their own inner disposition.
When speech is dogmatic and views are not broad, what was once considered perilous is instead transformed into something quite the opposite.
Regarding the alteration of the text from "encircling the left arm" (the *Gantong zhuan* cites it as "reaching the left arm"):
Bian states that while the original text says "encircling the left arm," the current reading of "reaching" is a reckless modification of the sacred words made to follow one's own views.
I have sought several editions of this *zhuan* throughout the past and present, and all state "encircling the left arm"; I hope that the Eastern Canon will preserve this.

The original text says "to reach" (*dá*) and does not say "to encircle" (*ráo*). This is because the single character "encircle" differs slightly from the character "reach," and thus it became the source of such arbitrary emendations.
I have previously seen the character written with the radical for "silk" (*miè*), making it "encircle.
What interpretation do you now hold that leads you to arbitrarily emend it? Even if one were to use the character "reach" to explain the text, it would still be external [to the intended meaning].
That which was criticized by non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) arose from this one corner [of the garment]; now it is suddenly eliminated. Thus, the transmitted text is revised to read:

"Reaching to the outer left arm. Where is that corner criticized by non-Buddhists now? Furthermore, the addition of the false application of fastenings and sleeves—what textual basis is there for such a view?
Moreover, the description is incomplete regarding the body; since the original purpose was to ward off the cold, that rationale no longer holds. It is merely...
Due to the arbitrary alteration of the character *ráo* (繞) to *dá* (達), beginners have become confused and follow suit without returning to the truth.

However, *dá* also carries the meaning of "to arrive. How can there be any "arriving" when [the robe] merely hangs at the chest? Knowing only how to attack what is different and dwell on shortcomings, the three robes barely cover half the body;
this is precisely what incurs the reproach of a "lewd woman" within the Vinaya. Now that these erroneous customs have fanned out...
I cannot bear to sit idly by and observe this; therefore, I shall further elaborate upon it, hoping that those who share my sentiments may take a look.

According to the *Gantong zhuan* (Biography of Spiritual Resonance), there are four reasons why the hem of the robe did not reach below the shoulders or down the arms, as detailed in the original biography.

Here, I shall briefly clarify the sequence in which these four conditions arose, followed by a brief explanation of the text of the biography. First, regarding the initial fashioning of the *kāṣāya*, the left arm [was left uncovered]...
Because women found it attractive, as a subsequent regulation, the robe was placed on the shoulder and weighted down with a sitting mat (*niṣīdana*).

Again, because of the sitting mat, the practitioner was ridiculed by non-Buddhists. Furthermore, because the corner of the robe rested upon the left arm, he was mocked for resembling an elephant’s trunk and the like.
Consequently, the corner of the robe was wrapped around the left arm. All of these were instances of being criticized due to the robe’s corner; such faults must not occur.
Because this was eliminated, the subsequent commentary states: "Now, one wraps the corner of the robe around the left arm and places it under the armpit" (meaning:

one takes the right corner of the robe, wraps it over the left upper arm, and then turns it back to place it under the left armpit; one must not let it hang down as before, nor let it hang from the left arm like an elephant's trunk).

It was for this reason that the hook-and-loop fastener was first instituted at the top [of the robe]. (For if the hook-and-loop fastener had not been installed, the robe would lack restraint and appear like that of a courtesan; by instituting the hook-and-loop fastener, these faults were avoided; hence it is said: "It was for this reason..."

This statement refers specifically to the wearing of the *saṃkakṣikā*. If one uses a modern-style robe with long and wide sleeves, it is said that wrapping the corners of the garment is inconvenient; however, one may simply tuck the right corner under the left arm beneath the robe, and thus avoid the transgression.
Some say that wearing the three robes in a layered manner is permitted by the Buddha.

If all three are made from old cloth—such that the *saṃghāṭī* has four layers and the middle and lower robes each have two layers—then since they must be worn in layers, they must necessarily be wrapped in layers as well; thus, the left...

Regarding the question that "if the corner of the robe on the arm is heavy and thick, it will not give rise to worldly goodness," the answer is: wrapping it around the left arm is merely to avoid the censure regarding the elephant's trunk;
one need only wrap the outermost layer to follow the transmitted texts and avoid the fault of over-wrapping.
Why must one specifically insist on using an old garment and thus create such an unnecessary difficulty? (The rest is as explained elsewhere).

Regarding the proposal to abolish the increased size of the sitting mat (the diagram states this, yet it is argued that while the principle of following the relaxation of the prohibition is generally permissible, one should merely add a maximum of half a *vitasti*;
how could the meager standards of the present day mean that the original measurement was insufficient?
Bian said: This is likely because [the critics] do not understand the Buddha’s subtle intent; thus, wishing to abolish the increased measurement on the grounds that Kāla’s body was large.

Regarding this text, I truly fear it may not be appropriate. Since the World-Honored One bestowed a single word or established a single precept, there has never been one intended for a single person that did not apply to others, nor one that covered only a single time without extending to future generations;

for the heart of the Greatly Compassionate and Benevolent One is universal and not limited. Furthermore, although Kāḷodāyin’s body was large, this merely served as a condition for increasing the measurement; it was simply added.
The measure of half a *vitasti* (span) is intended for application in the present and future worlds; it is not merely for the sake of Kātyāyana alone.

If one were to increase the measure solely based on Kātyāyana’s magnificent body, then this increased measure of a single precept would not only be inapplicable to the末代 (final age), but even during the Buddha’s lifetime, everyone outside of Kātyāyana’s body would be considered lowly and inferior—how could that be?

If one argues that it is improper to increase the size because it was lowly and crude at the time of its distribution, this would conversely contradict the World-Honored One’s establishment of the precepts;
why then restrict it to such a narrow view? Furthermore, there remains the transmission of the divine revelation from Central India to the Patriarch regarding the increase in size, which states:

"If one strictly adheres to the original measurement, it should indeed be restricted. However, those who do not sleep [in the robes] may possess them. The *Shō* (Commentary) cites the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya-śāstra* (Duolun).

The intention behind the rule for incremental measurement is clearly indicated by this teaching; thus the text states: "When the Buddha was in the world, there were many bhikṣus who did not lie down [on mats];

therefore, later on, it was permitted to increase the measurement by adding threads at the edges and so forth. Although the length and breadth of the sitting mat (niṣīdana) differ from those of our own school, what harm is there in the intention behind the incremental measurement?
Whether referring to sitting or lying down, both traditions are mentioned interchangeably. Some say that the *Shu-yao* (Commentary) cites the *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra*.

The intention behind this clarification is that since the *Sifen jieben* (Four-Part Prātimokṣa) and the *Shisong lü* (Ten Recitations Vinaya) differ—where the former says "one span" (*zhiji*) and the latter says "half a span" (*banzhi*)—I have cited them here for fear that people might use the terms incorrectly.
How could one take the underlying intent of those regulations as a proof?
In response, it is said: If the Patriarch [Daoxuan] intended merely to clarify that the *Jieben* texts differ for fear of misuse, he should have simply cited them directly.

Why must the passage concerning the different increments of length and width necessarily further cite the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* (or *Bahu-dharmaka-vinaya*) to explain its intent, following the text of the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya*?
One should know that the intent regarding the increments in the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* is stated solely with reference to sitting; it does not clarify the usage for lying down.
Therefore, the intent regarding the increments in the *Bahu-dharmaka-vinaya* is cited to clarify both meanings—sitting and lying down—showing that in both cases the sitting mat is to be spread out.
This is the meaning [of the distinction]. Furthermore, it is for the purpose of differentiating the various versions of the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* so that people do not mistakenly apply them.

In the commentary (*śāstra*), this distinction is maintained because the measurements of one *vitasti* (span) and half a *vitasti* differ according to the specific school (*nikāya*) and their respective traditions of observation;

consequently, there are variations in length and width. Therefore, the commentary uses these [measurements] to distinguish them so they are not used interchangeably. What harm is there if two schools add [different details]?

The measurement and the regulation of the mind refer to one and the same Buddha. If one relies on the text of the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*, it further provides its own commentary stating that "the knees do not emerge from the ground, nor do they remain raised";
this implies that there is no occasion for spreading out a sitting mat while lying down.
Some say that lying down is a sign of indolence and arrogance, and thus it is certainly not mentioned in the Vinaya; even if lying down were permitted, it would still not necessarily be the case.
One must spread out the sitting mat (*niṣīdana*). If one does not say "lying down," for what reason does the *Vinaya* state that one should "mindfully observe the light signs" (*ālokasamjñā*)?
Furthermore, why does the *Commentary* (*Chao*) cite the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, which states, "It is also permissible to fold the great robe (*saṃghāṭī*) four times and use it as a pillow"?

Moreover, if spreading the sitting mat were not permitted when lying down, how could the *Vinaya* text say, "For the sake of protecting the sitting mat"? The *Gantong zhuan* (*Senshūden*) also mentions the sitting mat.
The system for this was originally established to protect one’s own robes and the bedding of the Sangha. The *Jie-mo-su* (Karmavācanā-vyākhyā) states:

"Regarding 'for the sake of bedding,' it is because one fears damaging the property of the Sangha; thus, one intends to use it as a matting. Unless one has attained the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), how can one avoid being defiled by impurities?

Furthermore, in the lower volume of the *Chao* (Commentary), within the section on "Receiving Robes," under the entry for "single-layered bedding robes," the note says: "When spreading the bedding of the Sangha, one may let it hang down from the four sides of the bed."
Hanging down from each of the four corners is one *śaṭa* (one chi); upon it, one places the sitting mat (*niṣīdana*) and other items.

Since even those who possess a single-layered bedding cloth still place the sitting mat upon it, how much more so for those who lack such a cloth—how could one dare to judge that they may lie down without spreading the sitting mat? Now, as we are in this final age when faculties are dull, people lie down more often than they sit;
therefore, it is appropriate to increase the measurement. One should know that if one lies down, the mat must always be spread out; first, one must measure it.
Since all increments [of the *kathina* robe] are in accordance with the Dharma, why restrict them only to the present era? Why specifically abolish the increments?
Regarding the "filtering bag with a tied cord" (*nang yu xidai yi wu gouniu*):
as for the filtering bag having a tied cord on its handle, it is because one desires the convenience of keeping the bag securely in place; thus, the Teacher instructed people [to make it so].
It is merely a matter of being alert; if one is as clear-headed as this, why would one worry about wearing the three robes?
Why is the mind so clouded as to reach such a state? Furthermore, the purpose of the water-strainer is simply to filter water, and once its task is done, it is set aside.
The purpose of the three robes is simply to be worn, and when they are worn, they necessarily require hooks and ties. Since one is already capable of [this],...
If you pay such close attention to where the bag is stored, why do you not pay particular attention to where it is worn?
You can already be concerned about its use; yet, while being concerned about its use, you are not concerned that the concern itself is lax—is this not a case of being concerned about what is urgent?
I am not speaking in jest; rather, I observe the bag and its strap to discern the hook and the fastener, so that even if there were no immediate danger, one might discern the potential for danger.
Therefore, it is necessary to distinguish between them.

As for the texts such as the *Sū-cào* (Commentary-Excerpts) described by Nanshan [Daoxuan], which advocate the abolition of illustrated scriptures, they were likely written out of necessity due to the perceived inadequacies of ancient commentaries and excerpts.
Now, regarding the three robes and six requisites (*ṣaḍvastūni*), they have already appeared in the chapters on the two robes, the *Fuyi* (Ritual of Dressing), and other texts;

since these accounts are already complete, why has this "Diagram of the Six Requisites" also been produced? What is its intent? If it is because the texts in the chapter on robes and elsewhere are sufficient, then there would be no need to produce this text again.
Is it not the case that the teachings of Nanshan were insufficient for practice, and thus [this work] was written?
Shu Ye said, "Some say that because people today do not understand the regulations of the system, you have specifically drawn these diagrams and written this account.
I replied, "Now, one may possess the heart to benefit others but lack the skill to do so.

Furthermore, when a person observes a diagram to make clothing, even if they seek its measurements and proportions, they would not dare utter a single word regarding such things as the 'bird-foot' or 'horse-tooth' seams, or the front and back hooks and toggles."
Regarding such matters, how can one conceal them to show others? Furthermore, Dongzang (Dongchu) styled himself a *vinaya* master to propagate the ancestral Way;
yet, while he promoted and circulated commentaries and sub-commentaries throughout the world, why would he have feared that people would not understand the three robes and six requisites?
What Nanshan meant by "engaging in both facts and practice, without doubting sin or merit" is surely fully expressed in these texts and meanings; therefore, this work was composed.
It is said that this "Diagram of the Six Objects" (Liùwù tú) has now been published again and circulated separately in the world;
yet, as the formal methods are not fully prepared, those who cling to old ways often fail to consult the new text when examining the commentaries and sub-commentaries.

Is this not, in effect, an unwillingness to propagate the ancestral teachings? One might reply: "The commentaries and sub-commentaries are extensive and few people know them; therefore, I have now extracted their essential points."

I have compiled these matters into a single location so that the text is concise and easy to consult, ensuring that the regulations for the three robes and six requisites are heard throughout the world;

who then would say this is not so? As for the illustrations and diagrams, since their systems are found scattered across various texts, I have extracted their essential points and presented them here. I said:
"Have you not seen the *Zushi zhangfu* (The Robes and Vestments of the Patriarchs), the *Yijing chugao* (Yijing’s Edict on the Kitchen), and other such writings?"
Furthermore, regarding the text of this chart, who other than those versed in the Vinaya could have produced it at a single glance?
Now, does this chart and its text emerge from the Way of the Patriarchs? Or rather, one wonders about the intention behind the Patriarch’s composition:

why are the various textual meanings presented separately rather than collected in one place? It is likely because he wished for people to gain clear and thorough understanding through the commentaries and sub-commentaries.
It is not limited to a single aspect alone. Now that the diagrams have been lost, their system provides no benefit to people;

furthermore, the cited texts lead one astray from the essential teachings, thereby failing to capture the intent of the Patriarchs. Thus, from beginning to end, there is nothing of value here. As the ancients said, "To use one's own confusion to make others clear"—this is precisely what you have done.
If you could only relinquish your attachment to the ego and set aside this text, [the truth would be revealed].
Is it not fitting that those who have not yet attained clarity should be free from confusion regarding future generations? It is for this reason that I have spoken;
wishing for others to know the details of the *Sūcī* and the *Chāo*, I have not grudged the prolixity of these words.

Recently, while examining the *Liù wù tú* (Diagram of the Six Objects), I noticed that it had been secretly altered, expanded, and abridged, appearing as though the author had recently complied with advice (for instance, where "receiving" was not previously said to be threefold and "giving up" was not said to be single, these have now been added according to precedent).
As for the rest of the text’s meaning, stubborn attachments remain unremoved; thus, although one may say he has followed advice, he has not yet been able to flow with it like water.
Now, as the woodblocks are being carved, I am further concerned that later readers who consult this version might inadvertently adopt its secret alterations.
This was written to distinguish errors and refute falsehoods, thereby resolving doubts. Recorded on the day of the summer retreat in the third year of the Shaosheng era by the disciple Juecheng.
